analysis.one_liner: Mandates annual offshore oil and gas lease sales off North Carolina and shares drilling revenue with nearby coastal states.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee with zero cosponsors until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the Interior Department to hold an oil and gas lease sale off North Carolina's coast within two years, covering at least a quarter of the state's offshore federal waters, then once a year for five years [S2][S3]. It would send 37.5% of the money the federal government collects from these new leases — bonuses, rents, and royalties — to North Carolina, Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia, the four states within range of the drilling [S3]. It also blocks drilling that would interfere with military operations under an existing Defense-Interior agreement [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and never moved [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain the right to bid on and develop previously closed Atlantic waters off North Carolina, and the four coastal state governments would receive a guaranteed 37.5% share of all new lease revenue, no-strings-attached and without needing an appropriation [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies and four coastal state governments

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Secretary to hold an oil and gas lease sale off North Carolina within two years of enactment, covering at least 25% of the state's leasable offshore area, and to hold one sale each year for five years after that [S2][S3].

Amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to pay 37.5% of new offshore leasing revenue to North Carolina, Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia, allocated among states within 200 miles of a lease tract in inverse proportion to their distance from it; the nearest state gets at least 25% of the tract's payment [S3].
States can spend the money for any purpose under state law, without further appropriation, and it does not count as matching funds for federal programs [S3].

Prohibits drilling that would conflict with military operations under the 1983 Defense-Interior memorandum of agreement, and directs the two departments to update it for new technologies, including offshore wind [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The American public owns the offshore waters being leased; the bill would commit a public resource to private drilling on a fixed schedule regardless of market conditions, and coastal communities would bear the environmental and spill risk to fisheries, beaches, and tourism that could result [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the government's discretion: the Interior Department would have to hold lease sales on a rigid schedule even if drilling is uneconomic, risky, or opposed locally [S3].

New drilling off the Atlantic coast would put existing coastal economies — fisheries and beach tourism — at risk from spills and industrial activity, and the bill's military-protection clause constrains but does not eliminate exploration activity near training ranges [S2][S3].
Diverting 37.5% of new lease revenue to four states reduces the share of a publicly owned resource that returns to the federal Treasury, which funds programs for all taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The state revenue-sharing formula is genuinely generous and would have delivered real money to four coastal states, but only if companies actually bid and drilled — an outcome the bill tries to guarantee by mandate rather than let market conditions decide. The core of the bill is compulsory access to public waters for an industry that had been kept out of the Atlantic, with the public keeping a smaller share of the resource value and bearing the coastal risk. The tradeoff tilts toward the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee but never held a hearing or a vote, and the 114th Congress ended with the bill dead [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Richard Hudson (R-NC) introduced the bill on March 16, 2016, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S5].
On March 18, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed; no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed [S5].

The bill would have required an oil and gas lease sale off North Carolina within two years, annual sales for five years thereafter, and 37.5% of new offshore revenue paid to North Carolina, Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Atlantic waters stayed closed to oil and gas leasing. The oil and gas industry did not gain the access the bill was written to deliver, and coastal communities were not exposed to the drilling risk it would have created.

for.name: Rep. Richard Hudson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Natural Resources Committee; it was his sole sponsorship — no colleagues signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction, referred it to the Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: In its final five-year offshore leasing plan for 2017–2022, dropped proposed Atlantic drilling areas, which undercut the bill's premise that the Mid-Atlantic planning area would be leased.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so support beyond its one Republican sponsor never took shape in the chamber [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have compelled lease sales opening previously closed Atlantic waters off North Carolina to drilling, the access the industry had sought. The public would have received 37.5% of the resulting revenue through the four coastal states but kept a smaller federal share of a publicly owned resource and borne the coastal environmental risk [S3].

New drilling, and the seismic exploration that precedes it, off the North Carolina coast would expose the region's fishing grounds and beaches to spill and industrialization risk — the same coastline the industry's interest runs against [S2][S3].

industries.industry: State governments of North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, and Georgia
industries.note: The four states would receive 37.5% of all new offshore lease revenue, usable for any state purpose and guaranteed by formula rather than appropriation [S3].

industries.industry: Offshore wind and tidal energy developers
industries.note: The revenue-sharing provision covers wind and tidal energy on newly opened areas, and the bill directs the Defense and Interior departments to update their agreement for offshore wind technology — a small opening, though the bill's mandate is for oil and gas [S3].
